conclusion.label: rejects

report:
The claim that food-grade wax coatings on apples cause cancer is not supported by the evidence available.

Food-grade waxes used on apples—typically carnauba, shellac, and similar plant- or insect-derived substances—are applied after washing to replace the fruit's natural wax layer, which is removed during processing. These waxes are regulated as food additives, and their use is overseen by agencies like the FDA (https://www.fda.gov/). Toxicological safety assessments of common fruit waxes (carnauba, candelilla, beeswax, shellac) have found no evidence of carcinogenicity; these substances have long histories of safe use in cosmetics and food (https://www.cir-safety.org/sites/default/files/RR_Waxes.pdf).

Multiple fact-checking investigations directly address the viral cancer claim and find it unsubstantiated. Snopes examined a widely shared "shocking food industry secrets" video and found no known carcinogens in common fruit waxes, attributing the cancer claim to social media influencers who provide no scientific evidence (https://www.snopes.com/news/2018/09/18/breakdown-everything-wrong-shocking-secrets-food-industry-viral-video/). A separate fact-check by Vishvas News investigated a viral video claiming wax-coated apples could kill you and rated it misleading (https://www.vishvasnews.com/english/health/fact-check-can-consuming-wax-coated-apples-kill-you-misleading-video-getting-viral/). Food safety commentary consistently confirms the coatings are "generally safe for consumption," distinguishing legitimate food-grade wax from concerns about industrial wax adulteration in some markets (https://www.mashed.com/1761304/should-you-be-worried-about-wax-on-apples/).

Conclusion: There is no credible scientific or fact-checking evidence supporting the claim that food-grade apple wax causes cancer. This appears to be a persistent food myth driven by social media rather than by documented toxicological or epidemiological findings.
